opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot, because the models that give you the most world knowledge, the big vision-language models, were trained on internet data. That's mostly images and text. They've never seen a lidar point cloud or a radar return. But for driving at scale, those sensors really matter. Lidar gives you very precise geometry, radar gives you velocity and works well in fog and rain. You don't want to throw that away just because the pretrained backbone doesn't natively understand it.

So I think about it in a few layers. First, you can bring the new modality into the representation space the model already understands. You train an encoder for lidar or radar, and you align it, either directly to the vision-language embedding space or through some intermediate representation like a bird's-eye-view or object-level abstraction. The model can then consume these tokens alongside camera tokens. The key is that the alignment step can use a lot of paired data. We have huge amounts of synchronized camera and lidar logs, so you can learn that correspondence fairly well without needing labels for everything.

Second, there's the question of how much of the pretrained model you let change. If you fine-tune everything aggressively on driving data, you risk losing the general world knowledge that made you want the foundation model in the first place. So you're balancing adapters, partial fine-tuning, and co-training with the original kinds of data, so the model keeps its common sense while learning to use the new inputs.

Third, and this is where I think the field is heading, there's a split between a big model that reasons richly and maybe isn't fast enough to run on the car, and smaller, efficient models that run on board. The bigger model can be a teacher. It can fuse all modalities, generate auto-labels, and produce rich supervision. Then you distill that into the onboard system, which is natively built around your full sensor suite. So the foundation model's knowledge flows in, but the deployed system doesn't have to be literally the same network.

And finally, evaluation is critical. When you add a modality, you want to know it actually helps: in the long tail, in bad weather, at night, with partially occluded actors. You also want to know the model doesn't become over-reliant on one sensor and brittle when it degrades. So you test with sensor dropout and corruptions, and you lean heavily on simulation and closed-loop evaluation to see whether the behavior really gets better, not just the perception metrics.

So the short version is: align the new sensor into a shared representation, adapt carefully so you keep the world knowledge, use large models as teachers, and validate rigorously that the fused system is both better and more robust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding lidar or radar to a vision-language model, but does not draw an analogy to adding audio to a model initially trained on images.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually a really practical question, because it comes up all the time in autonomous driving. You build a system around a certain sensor suite, and then a new generation of hardware comes along, or you add a new type of lidar, or higher resolution cameras, or a different radar, and you don't want to throw away everything you've learned.

The way I think about it is that a foundation model for driving really has a few layers. There's the part that understands the world, the semantics of the scene, the agents, how they behave, the dynamics of traffic. And then there's the part that takes raw sensor data and maps it into that representation. The nice thing is that the world doesn't change when you change sensors. A pedestrian is still a pedestrian, an intersection still has the same structure. So most of the knowledge the model has is about the world, not about the specific sensor, and that knowledge should transfer.

So the key is to have an architecture where the sensor-specific pieces are relatively modular. You have encoders, or tokenizers if you want to think of it that way, for each modality, and they project into some shared latent space that the rest of the model operates on. When you get a new sensor, you train a new encoder for it that learns to produce embeddings in that same space, and you can do that with a lot less data than training from scratch, because the downstream model already knows what it expects to see. You can actually use the existing sensors as a teacher. If you have a vehicle that has both the old and the new sensors, you drive around and the old modalities give you a supervision signal for the new one, essentially a self-supervised alignment. You don't need labels for that.

Then there's the question of how much you let the rest of the model adapt. Typically you'd freeze most of it initially, train the new encoder, and then do some amount of fine-tuning end to end so the model actually learns to exploit what the new sensor is good at. Because if it just maps the new sensor into the old representation, you're sort of capping yourself at what the old sensors could express. A long-range lidar or a better radar sees things the old setup couldn't, and you want the model to take advantage of that.

The other thing I'd say is that this is one of the arguments for leaning on simulation and on generative models of the world. If you have a good model of the scene, you can render what a new sensor would see in existing logs, and that helps you bootstrap. It's not perfect, there's always a domain gap, but it gets you a lot of the way there.

And honestly, this is the big difference from the earlier era of self-driving, where every sensor change meant you retrained a whole pipeline of perception models and relabeled a lot of data. With a foundation model, the goal is that the expensive part, the world understanding, is sensor-agnostic, and adding a modality becomes a relatively cheap operation at the edges.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding sensors to a driving model, but does not compare it to adding audio to a model initially trained on images.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is where you introduce that modality and how much of the model you need to adapt. You may have a representation that already captures a lot about the world, learned from the existing sensors. You’d like to preserve that knowledge while giving the model a way to use the additional information.

One approach is to train an encoder for the new sensor and align its outputs with the representations the model already uses. Then you can gradually fine-tune the combined system. But I wouldn’t assume that you can just plug in a new encoder and everything downstream will work. If the sensor provides information the model has never had access to, some of those downstream components may need to change to take advantage of it.

And ultimately, you have to evaluate whether the system actually uses that information effectively. Does it resolve ambiguities? Does it improve behavior in difficult situations? What happens when that sensor is unavailable or degraded? Those are the questions that tell you whether you’ve successfully incorporated the modality.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding a new sensor modality and adapting the model, but does not compare this to adding audio to a model initially trained on images.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate what the model understands about the world from how a particular sensor observes it. If you’ve learned a useful representation of the scene—where things are, how they’re moving, how they might interact—you’d like a new sensor to contribute to that representation without having to learn everything again from scratch.

One approach is to train an encoder for the new modality, using synchronized observations to align its outputs with the representations the existing model already uses. You can initially keep much of the model fixed, then fine-tune more broadly as needed. But you don’t want alignment to throw away the information that makes the new sensor useful. It may observe something the other sensors cannot, so the shared representation may need to evolve as well.

And then there’s the question of whether the downstream system actually uses that information correctly. Recognizing an object more reliably doesn’t automatically translate into better driving. You have to evaluate the effect on prediction and planning, including situations where sensors disagree or one becomes unavailable. So I’d view this as reusing a strong foundation, while still validating the complete driving system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding a new sensor modality and aligning its representation, but it does not draw the specific analogy to adding audio to a model initially trained on images.
